messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur, a 52-year-old film director, had always thrived in the chaotic energy of a film set. That changed eighteen months ago during a night shoot for a dramatic thriller. He was in the dark, overseeing a complex crane operation when a critical rigging component catastrophically failed. The deafening crash of falling equipment, followed by a blinding flash of sparks and the screams of injured crew, etched itself into his mind. Though physically unharmed, Arthur found himself trapped in a new reality.

In the aftermath, his mind replayed the incident with terrifying clarity. His memories of the frightening event were mostly pictures or images – the collapsing metal, the desperate faces, the sudden darkness – vivid and detailed, yet he couldn't seem to put the experience into words. It felt like a reel constantly looping, but without a script. These persistent, nonverbal recollections began to erode his sense of self. He found himself increasingly convinced that he was inadequate, a "bad coper" whose reactions since the event showed he was simply lousy at handling crisis. The person he had become felt utterly unrecognisable to him, a hollowed-out version of his former self.

What frightened Arthur most was the constant, gnawing sense of danger. The vivid, visual memories of the accident kept him on edge, making him hypervigilant, superalert and watchful. Any unexpected or loud sounds now sent a jolt through him, leaving him on high alert, scanning his surroundings. He found himself jumping or startling at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people – the sudden clatter of a prop on set, a car backfiring outside his editing suite, even the doorbell at home. This constant state of heightened threat became unbearable, and in response, Arthur began to avoid circumstances that reminded him of the event. He started turning down night shoots, refusing to work in enclosed, dark spaces, and even found himself steering clear of sets with complex rigging. He also found himself trying to distract himself with something else whenever the memories surfaced, or pondering why the event had happened to him, though these thoughts rarely brought comfort or clarity.

His avoidance, however, only tightened the loop of his suffering. Because he was constantly on guard and startling at sounds, he increasingly avoided any situation that might trigger these reactions, including his own film sets. This withdrawal, in turn, reinforced his negative self-perceptions; every cancelled meeting or declined project was further proof that he was indeed a lousy coper and inadequate, deepening the belief that the person he had become was unrecognisable. His partner, Maria, noticed his increasing isolation, the way he would suddenly freeze at a car horn, or how he insisted on leaving every light on in their apartment after dusk. By avoiding the very environments where he might confront his fears and gradually disconfirm the perceived threat, Arthur inadvertently maintained his hypervigilance. The less he exposed himself to the realities of a working set, the more dangerous it felt in his mind, and the more these avoidance behaviours confirmed his belief that he was fundamentally broken.

Arthur had come to a point where his career, his relationship, and his very identity felt hostage to the accident. He finally sought help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the director he once was, terrified that he might never escape the tightening grip of his own mind.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not explicitly state that Arthur's negative self-appraisals directly cause or lead to his maladaptive coping strategies.
The vignette does not establish a causal link where Arthur's negative self-appraisals directly contribute to his sense of threat or hypervigilance.
The vignette describes maladaptive strategies as responses to memories or threat, but not as a cause or influence on the presence or nature of the intrusive memories themselves.
